# An Anomaly and Monitoring Pipeline

Build a pipeline that flags unusual values and detects drift in a time series
(e.g., a flood spike in a river gauge, or a pollution spike at a study site)
using z-scores and rolling statistics. A distinct kind of analysis: monitoring
and anomaly detection.

-   An anomaly is an observation far from what a model expects.
-   Z-scores and rolling statistics define "expected" and "far".
-   Drift means the data's baseline itself is moving.
-   Monitoring runs continuously, so it must be cheap and logged.

-   Import the tools this lesson needs. `statistics` comes from the standard
    library; `polars` and `altair` do the heavy lifting. We fix the seed so the
    synthetic series, spike, and flags are identical on every run.

{{< inc anomaly/anomaly.py mark=import >}}

-   A river gauge is a time series: one number per timestamp. We synthesize a
    week of hourly readings as a flat baseline plus small noise, then inject one
    brief flood spike. Real data would arrive from an ingest step; here we make
    it ourselves so the lesson is self-contained.

{{< inc anomaly/anomaly.py mark=generate >}}

-   An anomaly is an observation far from what a model expects. Our first model
    is "the level is usually the mean, give or take the standard deviation". A
    z-score measures distance from that mean in units of standard deviation:
    zero is average, 3 is three standard deviations out.

{{< inc anomaly/anomaly.py mark=z_scores >}}

-   Flag any point whose z-score is outside three standard deviations. Taking
    the absolute value catches both a spike and a sudden drop, since either is
    unusual.

{{< inc anomaly/anomaly.py mark=flag >}}

-   Only the four spike points clear the threshold; the noise is well inside it.
    We flag rather than drop: an anomaly is a signal to inspect, not an error to
    remove.

{{< inc anomaly/anomaly.py mark=plot >}}

-   The plot puts a red dot on each flagged reading, exactly on the spike. But
    the global mean and standard deviation are fixed. If the river's usual level
    slowly rises, "expected" has moved and every new reading starts to look
    unusual. That movement is drift, and rolling statistics track it.

{{< inc anomaly/anomaly.py mark=rolling >}}

-   The rolling version flags only the leading edge of the spike. A window that
    contains the spike absorbs it into its own mean and standard deviation, so
    the trailing points look ordinary again. Rolling statistics follow a slow
    baseline well and catch a single sharp jump poorly. In practice you keep
    both models: a global one for the usual level and a rolling one for drift.

-   Monitoring runs continuously, so each check must be cheap. A rolling mean
    and standard deviation update in constant time from a couple of running
    sums, and need only the last few readings, not the whole history. Every
    alert is logged with its readings, window, and threshold, so it can be
    traced back and replayed.

-   The same pipeline runs on the ecology example with only the column changed:
    swap `level` for `pollution_ppm`, and a pollution spike at a study site is
    flagged the same way.
